title: adaptive-checkpointing-and-bandwidth-elasticity-casebook
body:
Purpose
This note collects exploratory experiments and heuristics for a new approach we prototyped: adaptive page-granularity checkpointing (APC) combined with a lightweight metric we call Bandwidth Elasticity Index (BEI). Goal is to reduce long-tail token latencies and reduce NVMe/PCIe microburst spillback that correlates with high eviction churn in multi-tenant mixed-seqlen workloads.

High-level hypothesis
- Many 99th+ tail events are triggered not by single large evictions but by rapid oscillation between small spillbacks and immediate prefetches (a thrash cycle).
- If we checkpoint hot page groups at page-granularity during steady periods (cheap writebacks of residency metadata + optional small persistence), we can avoid full reclaim + readback during transient surges.
- BEI (defined below) provides an online signal for when to open/close checkpoint windows per slot to maximize reuse without increasing steady-state BW.

What is BEI (Bandwidth Elasticity Index)
- Intuition: measure how much instantaneous BW headroom is available relative to recent sustained throughput.
- Implementation (prototype): BEI = (p99(read_bw + write_bw, 1s) - mean(read_bw + write_bw, 10s)) / mean(read_bw + write_bw, 10s) clipped to [-1, +3].
- Positive BEI => short-lived headroom (safe to issue prefetches); Negative BEI => saturated channel, must throttle checkpointing/prefetch.
- Chosen windows intentionally asymmetric (1s p99 vs 10s mean) to capture microbursts.

Bench harness and workloads
- bench name: bench-churn-v2 (small extension of bench-churn with mixed seqlen mix and injected synthetic bursts)
- tenants: 12 concurrent tenants on 4-GPU node (A100x4-80GB equivalent).
- workload profiles: 60% chat-short (seqlen ~64), 30% long-context retrievals (seqlen ~4096 but sparse kv accesses), 10% embedding & rerank bursts.
- Injected arrival spikes: poisson baseline with periodic 250ms burst windows (16x arrival rate).
- Telemetry captured: per-slot kv-residency, page read/write counts, PCIe DMA queue depth, NVMe latencies, per-request tail latencies, LRU churn count.

Experiment summaries (not exhaustive)
1) Baseline (no APC, current prefetch/paging heuristics)
- Result: frequent small writes to NVMe during bursts; read amplification high (1.7x) due to immediate re-read of recently-evicted pages. 99p token latency shows pronounced spikes aligned with burst windows.
- Observed correlated signal: NVMe write IOPS spikes shortly before read IOPS, suggesting prefetchs triggered too late.

2) Naive APC (global checkpoint window open for all slots during bursts)
- Result: lowered read amplification slightly but caused increased steady-state NVMe writes (30% uplift) leading to sustained elevated queueing and worse 95p latency. Conclusion: naive global checkpointing trades short-term tail for worse steady-state latency.

3) APC + BEI gating (per-slot adaptive windows)
- Heuristic: open checkpoint window for slot S if: reuse_rate(S, 30s) > 0.12 AND BEI > 0.25; close window if BEI < -0.05 OR reuse_rate decays below 0.08. Checkpoint ops are rate-limited to max 2 pages/sec per slot aggregated by slot-group.
- Result: 99p token latency reduced by ~28% vs baseline on burst workloads, steady-state NVMe write uplift limited to ~6%. Read amplification fell to 1.1x.
- Notes: tuning BEI thresholds critical across hardware types.

4) Sequence-length-aware window sizing
- Idea: longer context requests have more predictable KV access patterns; we used larger checkpoint windows for slots dominated by long-context traffic.
- Result: small additional improvement for mixed workload (3-5% 99p).

Telemetry artifacts and traces
- Example trace: bench-churn-v2 run #17 (attached as trace id INF-3421-run17) shows BEI positive spikes preceding successful checkpointing events that avoid readback. Slack thread includes quick screenshots.
- Important counters to capture in prod: per-slot BEI, slot_checkpoint_state, checkpoint_issued_pages_per_min, nvme_write_95p_latency, pci_queue_depth_99p.

Open questions / risks
- Consistency: checkpointing residency metadata must not change eviction semantics in unexpected ways (we validated on synthetic workloads but need more regressions).
- Write amplification across tenants: aggregated APC might increase wear on NVMe in heavy tenants; need cross-tenant rate-capping and accounting.
- Security/compliance: if checkpointing writes persisted state, ensure it does not violate private deployment data residency guarantees; in our prototype we keep written pages encrypted and metadata-only (no user data).
- BEI calibration: thresholds depend on underlying HW and model mix; we need an automatic calibration job (see TODOs).

Operational playbook (draft)
- Default: APC off for hosted tier; enable per-customer in Dedicated with opt-in until calibration stable.
- Monitoring: BEI heatmap, checkpoint window open-rates, nvme_writes_by_tenant. Add alert if nvme_write_95p_5m > baseline*1.4.
- Fallback: if persistent write latencies cross safe threshold, automatically revert APC per-node.

Implementation notes / PRs
- Prototype code live in runtime branch: feature/apc-bei-proto (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1289).
- New perf counters implemented in perf/telemetry: slot.bei, slot.checkpoint_rate.
- Small kernel interaction: efficient page-group writeback implemented as fused DMA ops (microbench in perf/benchmarks/dma-fuse-v2).

Next steps and experiments planned
- Long-duration runs across 72h to measure NVMe wear and steady-state write amplification.
- Run on multiple instance types: PCIe gen3 vs gen4 vs NVLink-local to measure BEI stability.
- Auto-calibration job: use 4 warmup runs per node to find BEI thresholds per model mix.
- Cross-tenant fairness: simulate skewed tenant with heavy prefetch demand to validate aggregate rate-limiter.

Quick TODOs
- [ ] Add BEI calculation into prod aggregator (Sasha)
- [ ] Add per-tenant checkpoint accounting to billing/ops metrics (Miguel)
- [ ] Run 72h bench-churn-v2 on gen4 hardware and capture NVMe SMART histograms (David)

Random notes / scratchpad
- Observed an odd anomaly where BEI measured positive but NVMe write queueing still high; traced to PCIe scheduler starvation on one host (investigate driver scheduler QoS interaction).
- Consider alternative BEI variants: use 500ms p95 vs 30s median; or incorporate DMA queue depth directly. Might experiment next sprint.

Conclusions (working)
APC gated by an elasticity signal (BEI) looks promising: meaningful reduction in tail latency for bursty mixes with bounded steady-state write cost. The gating and rate-limits are essential; naive checkpointing worsens steadiness. Next milestone: production-safe calibration and a 72h stability run on dedicated nodes.
